scoreNote: Strong (5): grants that questioning is essential, then qualifies the absolute always by showing that foundations must first be absorbed and that questioning must be selective; clear and well argued.

sentences.text: A good education is meant to produce independent thinkers rather than parrots, so the call for students to question what they are taught has obvious appeal.
The statement urges students to always question their lessons rather than accept anything passively.
Questioning is indeed essential to real learning, but the word always pushes a sound principle too far, because some knowledge must first be absorbed before it can be intelligently questioned at all.
It is true that passive acceptance is the enemy of genuine understanding.
A student who merely memorizes and repeats has learned to obey rather than to think, and forgets the material the moment the exam ends.
The great advances of science and reform came from people who refused to accept received wisdom, from Galileo questioning the heavens to reformers questioning unjust laws.
Questioning forces a student to understand why something is true, to find its limits, and to own the knowledge rather than merely rent it.
A classroom that rewards obedience over curiosity produces graduates who can recite but cannot reason.
Progress in almost every field began with someone unwilling to take the textbook's word for it.
In this respect the statement is plainly right: questioning is the engine of understanding.
However, to question everything always is neither possible nor wise.

A beginner cannot meaningfully question calculus before learning arithmetic, or debate history before learning what happened, because the raw materials of thought must be acquired before they can be challenged.
There is a stage in every subject when a student must trust the teacher enough to absorb the basics, just as an apprentice copies before he creates.
To demand that a child question the multiplication table or the spelling of words is not independence but paralysis.
No one reinvents mathematics from scratch before daring to use it.
Even the boldest critic must stand on a great deal of knowledge he has simply accepted on trust.
Acceptance, at the right moment, is not passivity but the foundation on which later questioning is built.
Moreover, the value lies not in questioning constantly but in questioning well.
Reflexive doubt that challenges everything indiscriminately is as lazy as blind acceptance, merely contrarian rather than thoughtful.

vocab.gloss: 為反對而反對的；唱反調的

sentences.text: The educated mind knows when to absorb and when to interrogate, trusting established knowledge while staying alert to its weaknesses.
Real critical thinking is selective: it spends its skepticism where it is warranted rather than scattering it everywhere at once.
To question wisely, a student must first know enough to tell a real weakness from an imagined one.
Wisdom is knowing which lessons to question and which to learn first.
In conclusion, students should question what they are taught, but not always and not everything at once.
They should absorb the foundations a subject requires and then question actively as their understanding grows, treating acceptance and inquiry as stages rather than enemies.
Curiosity without foundations is mere noise; foundations without curiosity are dead weight.
The goal is not a student who doubts everything, but one who knows when to learn and when to challenge.
